title: I Took the Pretzel-Kettle Booking to the Baker Who Left My Numbered Lye

parts.text: I stepped into the kettle bay at 6:04 a.m. and baker Otto was already using numbered gear. The board said: ONE KETTLE. FORTY MINUTES. LYE STAYS WITH THE BOOKING. I was twenty-eight, kitchen secretary, holding a checkout that listed our numbered lye. Otto shrugged. "Bakers are the kettle." I photographed the board, the booking, and his leftover dip on my numbered lye. Then I asked for the kettle log. At 6:12 the bay pinged why Otto's name was on my dip. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The bay can see Otto's leftover dip on my numbered lye.

social.video_title: He left my numbered pretzel lye on my kettle — Part 1/2
social.description: Kettle bay, leftover dip, a forty-minute clock he posted. I logged the lye. Would you have asked for the kettle log?

parts.text: Otto called it extra dip until the bay asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the dip still. The lye went back to my numbered booking. Otto ran a slot of his own and told the next baker atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: BAKERS ARE NOT THE KETTLE. I keep my lye in a labeled jug. Otto brown-bags his dip. The bay finally looks like a booking, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.description: Kettle log, numbered lye, and a second line on the board. Was extra dip ever my lye?
